```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ny_noaa = read_csv("./data/nynoaadat.csv")

#check dimension name and data structure
dim(ny_noaa)
names(ny_noaa)
glimpse(ny_noaa)
```
```{r}
#check missing value
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ sum(is.na(.))
    )
  )
```
#By observing the result, we can get that the NY NOAA dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. It includes weather station IDs, dates, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. The dataset contains character, date, and numeric variables. Missing data is an important issue, especially for maximum and minimum temperatures, which both have about 43.7% missing values. Snow depth has 22.8% missing values, while snowfall and precipitation have 14.7% and 5.6% missing values, respectively. Station IDs and dates have no missing values.


#Problem 2
```{r}
nhanes_covar = read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv")

nhanes_accel = read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv")

# Check dimensions
dim(nhanes_covar)
dim(nhanes_accel)

# Check variable names
names(nhanes_covar)
names(nhanes_accel)

# Check data structure
glimpse(nhanes_covar)
glimpse(nhanes_accel)
```
```{r}
#better show the data
nhanes_covar = read_csv(
  "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4,
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    seqn = as.numeric(seqn),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    !is.na(seqn),
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(bmi),
    !is.na(education)
  )

glimpse(nhanes_covar)
dim(nhanes_covar)
```
```{r}
#merge data
nhanes_accel = nhanes_accel |>
  janitor::clean_names()

glimpse(nhanes_accel)

nhanes_merged = nhanes_covar |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")

dim(nhanes_merged)
```
```{r}
# Tidy accelerometer data
nhanes_tidy = nhanes_merged |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(
      stringr::str_remove(minute, "min")
    )
  )

# Check the data
dim(nhanes_tidy)
glimpse(nhanes_tidy)
```
#(b) create the table we need
```{r}
# Count participants by education and sex
education_table = nhanes_tidy |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, education) |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  education_table,
  caption = "Number of Men and Women by Education Level"
)
```
# There are 228 participants, including 118 men and 110 women. Most participants have more than a high school education (115 participants). Men and women have similar counts in the lowest and highest education groups, while the high school equivalent group has more men than women.

```{r}
# Age distribution by sex and education, here we use a boxplot
nhanes_covar |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
# The age distributions differ across education levels. Participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger than those in the other groups. In the high school equivalent group, women have a higher median age than men. In the less than high school group, men and women have similar age distributions.

```{r}
# Calculate total daily activity
nhanes_total = nhanes_tidy |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Check results
dim(nhanes_total)
head(nhanes_total)
```
```{r}
# Plot total daily activity against age
nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = age,
    y = total_activity,
    color = sex
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```
#The plot shows that total daily activity generally decreases as age increases. This pattern appears in all three education groups. Men and women have similar overall trends, although women tend to have higher activity levels in some age ranges. The group with more than high school education shows a relatively gradual decrease in activity, while the other two groups show more variation. Overall, age appears to be related to daily activity, but there are also differences between individuals.


```{r}
#final step of problem 2
# Calculate average activity for each minute
nhanes_hourly = nhanes_tidy |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

# Check results
dim(nhanes_hourly)
head(nhanes_hourly)
```
```{r}
# Plot 24-hour activity patterns
nhanes_hourly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.15
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
#The plot shows that daily activity follows a similar pattern across all three education groups. Activity is lowest during the early morning, around 3–5 AM, and increases quickly after 6 AM. Activity is generally highest during the daytime and decreases again in the evening. Women tend to have higher activity levels than men during the day, especially in the group with more than high school education. The group with less than high school education has a higher peak around noon, while the other groups show more stable daytime activity. Overall, daily activity patterns are similar across education levels, but there are some differences between men and women.


#Problem 3
```{r}
# Import cvs
citi_jan_2020 = read_csv("./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")
citi_july_2020 = read_csv("./data/July 2020 Citi.csv")
citi_jan_2024 = read_csv("./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")
citi_july_2024 = read_csv("./data/July 2024 Citi.csv")
```
```{r}
# Check dimensions
dim(citi_jan_2020)
dim(citi_july_2020)
dim(citi_jan_2024)
dim(citi_july_2024)

# Check variable names
names(citi_jan_2020)
names(citi_july_2020)
names(citi_jan_2024)
names(citi_july_2024)

# Check data structure
glimpse(citi_jan_2020)
glimpse(citi_july_2020)
glimpse(citi_jan_2024)
glimpse(citi_july_2024)
```

```{r}
# Combine Citi Bike datasets
citi_bike = bind_rows(
  citi_jan_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
  citi_july_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
  citi_jan_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
  citi_july_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
)
# Clean and organize variables
citi_bike = citi_bike |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2020, 2024)),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member")
    )
  )
# Check the combined dataset
dim(citi_bike)
glimpse(citi_bike)

# Check missing values
colSums(is.na(citi_bike))

# Check ride duration
summary(citi_bike$duration)
```
```{r}
# Count rides by year, month, and membership
citi_summary = citi_bike |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarize(
    n_rides = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n_rides
  )

# Display reader-friendly table
knitr::kable(
  citi_summary,
  caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
)
```
# Citi Bike members took more rides than casual riders in all four months. July had more rides than January in both 2020 and 2024. The number of rides increased from 2020 to 2024, with July 2024  having the highest number of rides. This suggests that Citi Bike usage is higher in summer and has grown over time.

```{r}
# Find top 5 starting stations in July 2024
top_stations = citi_bike |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(start_station_name, name = "n_rides", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

# Display table
knitr::kable(
  top_stations,
  caption = "Top 5 Starting Stations in July 2024"
)
```
# Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station in July 2024, with 163 rides. The other four stations had between 146 and 155 rides. The differences among the top five stations were relatively small.

```{r}
# Calculate median ride duration
citi_median = citi_bike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Check results
head(citi_median)
```
```{r}
# Plot median ride duration
citi_median |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = month,
    group = month
  )) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Citi Bike Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
# Median ride durations were higher in July than in January for both 2020 and 2024. Weekend rides were generally longer, especially in July. Median ride durations were also higher in 2020 than in 2024 across all weekdays.

```{r}
# Filter 2024 data
citi_2024 = citi_bike |>
  filter(year == 2024)

# Create boxplots
citi_2024 |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = rideable_type,
    y = duration,
    fill = member_casual
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.alpha = 0.15
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Bike Type, Membership, and Month in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Membership"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```
# Casual riders generally had longer ride durations than members. Ride durations were usually higher in July than in January, especially for casual riders using classic bikes. Casual riders on classic bikes tended to ride longer than those on electric bikes. There were also many long-duration outliers, especially in July.
